title: Guide to field note-taking
text:
You will have to keep track of a lot of information. You are less likely to lose track of that information if you set up your notebook so that you won’t forget.






Prep for each field day!



You will relieve pressure on your morning if you are able to prepare for class the night before. This includes your notebook! Before heading out, you can list the important metadata to have, format your pages, etc. so that by the time you are in the field, all you have to do is fill in the information.

title: Guide to field note-taking
text:
Notebook organization
Every field day, you will be recording your observations in your notebook. Your field notebook is the repository for all the information you will be learning in the field. It is very important to keep it organized!
Each field day should include:

Metadata
Species account
Observations and field notes
Post-field day reflection

Your species account and observations with field notes will be completed in class. Your post-field day reflection will be done outside of class.

title: Guide to field note-taking
text:
Metadata
“Metadata” is information about information. Metadata provides broad context for the information you record in your notebook. For each field day, you should record:

Date
Time (start and end)
Location
Number of people in group
Weather (qualitative description)

title: Guide to field note-taking
text:
Species accounts
In the field, we will walk around and identify organisms of varying taxonomic groups to get a sense of how a habitat or ecosystem is structured.
Your species account should be organized in a table; you can draw this in your notebook prior to the field day so that you can keep track of the species we discuss.
Each species account section should be organized with the following information in organized columns:

species
number of individuals
identifying characteristics
behavior, phenology, location, etc.
notes







Priorities in the field



You may find that your notes get messy when you’re taking down information in the field. That is ok! If your species accounts get messy, take time after class to copy your notes onto clean pages in your notebook.
You will receive feedback to incorporate this practice into your maintenance of your field notebook during the notebook checks if your species accounts are particularly messy.

title: Guide to field note-taking
text:
Observations and field notes
Field notes and observations are the core of this class. Good notes document species observations (what did you see), behaviors/trends/phenomena (what was it doing), and the context for those observations (where did you see what you saw, at what time of day/year). Field notes also signify what you think is important to document; you are assigning value to information when you’re deciding whether or not to write it down.
Above all, field notes must be honest and accurate. This means that you have documented what you have sincerely tried to understand as true, incorporating information from your own perspective, others’ perspectives, and other sources of information (e.g. field guides, literature).

title: Guide to field note-taking
text:
Post-field trip reflection
Each field trip should be accompanied by a reflection, which takes the form of a diary format chronicling the trip using information from the notes you take in the field (this is why it’s important to keep good field notes!).
Each reflection should start with the date and time you complete the reflection (I recommend the same-day or day after, when things are fresh in your memory).
The content of the reflection should include:

A narrative account of the trip: where we went at the site, where we stopped to conduct detailed observations, etc.
New experiences for you: for example, a new organism, drawing, conversation with someone in the class, identification, etc.
How you improved in a skill: for example, drawing a diagram, composing an observation page, keeping track of all your personal items, etc.

All reflections should be done in your field notebook.

title: Methods of promoting observations
text:
Source credit



Much of the inspiration for note-taking and observation comes from common note-taking methods in ecological disciplines and John Muir Laws’s The Guide to Nature Drawing and Journaling. If you’re interested in borrowing this text, let me know!
The information on this page comes from two sources by John Muir Laws: The Guide to Nature Drawing and Journaling and Opening the World Through Nature Journaling.
If you’re interested in developing your journaling practice further, I would highly recommend John Muir Laws’s work! He has many free videos walking through observation techniques, drawing, composition, etc.

title: Methods of promoting observations
text:
Promoting observation

I notice…
Examine whatever you are looking at. Start to say observations out loud. Do not filter anything out: if you see it, say it. Look at structure, behavior, color, interactions. Change your perspective: look up close or far away and see what else you can observe. If you find yourself running out of observations, challenge yourself to discover something new, or just say “I notice. . .” until an idea pops out. Pay attention to what surprises you. This gives you insight into ways that the world is different than you had thought.


I wonder…
After observing your object, start to come up with questions about it and say those out loud, too. Your questions might be connected to an observation you made earlier, or they could be about any aspect of what you’re observing. There is no need to worry about answering the questions yet. Just get them all out there. It’s okay if you continue to make-and say-observations as you come up with questions.


It reminds me of…
Last, say out loud everything that your object reminds you of. Allow yourself to be uninhibited in this step. Say anything that comes to mind: the object may have jarred your memory, reminding you of an experience you’ve had or a piece of information you already know, or the way it looks physically might remind you of something. Try looking at individual parts of the object, then back up and examine it as a whole.

title: Methods of promoting observations
text:
Interrogatives

Who: identity and identification
“Who made this nest?” “What kind of bird is that?”


What: describing events, trends, phenomena, behaviors
“What foraging strategies is this bird using?” “What is happening here?” “What happens when the sun comes out?”


Where: location (local and large scale)
“Do I spot this species at the forest edge or deep in the woods?” “Is this bird a resident or is it migrating?” “Where is it going next?” “Where will it spend the night?” “Is this nest hole oriented for protection from the wind or water?”
When: timing and phenology “What part of the nesting cycle are we in?” “How does the approaching winter play into what the bird is doing right now?” “How long can this cormorant hold its breath?” “How long does it take for the newt to crawl over a log?” “When did the flower turn into the fruit?”


How: mechanism or process
“How do those pelicans fly so close to the water without hitting the surface?” “How do bustits weave such delicate nests?”


Why: reason or meaning
“Why are the wings tilted up?” “Why are the leaves glossy?” “Why are these two individuals growing in such different locations?”
“Why” questions can be asked of any observation and are a good follow-up to other questions, to push inquiry deeper.

title: Interaction diagram
text: Due Tuesday 6 October at the beginning of class

title: Interaction diagram
text:
Overview
This is the second of five project prep assignments for the field guide assignment. Previously, you selected two site × taxonomic group combinations and described why you were interested in those sites/groups. In this assignment, you will explore the potential relationships between species you selected and other species that may occur at that site. You will depict relationships between species using an interaction diagram that will ultimately appear in your final field guide.
All components of this assignment should be done by hand on paper.

title: Interaction diagram
text:
Before starting this assignment

Read “Direct and Indirect Interactions” by Moon, Daniel C. et al. from Nature Education Knowledge.
Read the species descriptions for your species in the appropriate field guide or textbook. This may include (but is not limited to):

plants: The Jepson Manual edited by BG Baldwin, California Plants by Matt Ritter, A Californian’s guide to the trees among us by Matt Ritter
birds: Field guide to Birds of Western North America by Sibley
reptiles: Field Guide to Amphibians and Reptiles of California by Stebbins and McGinnis
mammals: Mammals of North America by Kays and Wilson
invertebrates: Field Guide to California Insects by Will, Gross, Rubinoff, and Powell








Use library resources!



All the books listed above are available in hard copy or online via the library.

title: Interaction diagram
text:
Assignment

1. Draw and describe one ecological relationship for each of your taxonomic groups.
Choose one pair of species from each taxonomic group. Consider the flow of energy between both species. For each pair, draw the appropriate arrows connecting the two species in the pair.
For each pair, explain in 2-3 sentences why you drew the interaction in that way, using information about the morphology, phenology, habitat, and/or behavior of each species. Be specific about the characteristics you used to categorize the interaction. Provide citations for information about species characteristics and any other details you found from the literature.


2. Draw interaction diagrams between all the species you chose for each taxonomic group.
You should have two interaction diagrams - one for each group - with arrows connecting each species. With new species, the flow of energy may change from the diagram you drew in part 1 (though it may stay the same!).
For each diagram, explain in 2-3 sentences why you think those interactions exist, using characteristics of each species to justify your thinking. As above, be specific about the characteristics you used to categorize the interaction and provide citations.


3. Draw interaction diagrams incorporating three new species not included in your core species list.
Recreate each diagram you drew in part 2 with two additional species outside of your focal taxonomic group.
For each diagram, explain in 3-5 sentences - how and why you chose the new species - how the diagram has changed with the addition of the new species
Be specific about the characteristics of the species that inform your choice of interaction. Provide citations as needed.

title: Interaction diagram
text:
Checklist
By the due date, you should have:

drawings and written responses for part 1
drawings and written responses for part 2
drawings and written responses for part 3

As a reminder: all components of this assignment should be done by hand in pen, pencil, or other writing implement on paper. You will turn in the paper copy of your work in class on Tuesday.

title: Site and species selection
text: Due Friday 2 October at 11:59 PM on Canvas

title: Site and species selection
text:
Project overview
This is the first of five project prep assignments for the field guide assignment. Your final field guide will be a guide to the 5 most common species in a given taxonomic group at the site of your choosing.

title: Site and species selection
text:
Assignment

1. Familiarize yourself with the sites we will visit in this class.
You can find a list of sites on the syllabus and on the site selection spreadsheet.


2. Sign up for two site × taxonomic group combinations.
For this and following steps, you will explore your options for two site × taxonomic group combinations. Your selections are not set in stone; however, you should give yourself the flexibility to explore two groups to ultimately choose one later on.


3. Articulate your reasoning for your choices.
In 1-3 sentences, describe:

why you are interested in these sites, with specific references to your own interests in ecosystems, experience, etc.
why you are interested in these taxonomic groups, again with specific references to your own interests
why you want to explore the taxonomic groups you chose at the sites you chose
how you personally might be able to transport yourself to these sites, if you needed to visit them (e.g. via bus, car, etc.) - be realistic about this!



4. Find the 5 most common species in each group at your chosen site(s).
Using iNaturalist, eBird, or any other observation database, find the most common species in your taxonomic group of choice at your sites.
For each site × taxonomic group combination, you should:

make a list of the 5 most common species
describe in 1-3 sentences how you found those species (for example, what filters or processes on iNaturalist did you use)

title: Site and species selection
text:
Checklist
By the due date, you should have:

signed up for two site × taxonomic group combinations
addressed the points in part 3 and 4 in a Word or Google doc
uploaded your written responses to the Canvas portal
